Expansion of game sanctuaries 
*162. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to extend the land area under 
game sanctuaries by buying up adjacent land; 
(b) whether it is a fact that ther e is a need to extend the area 
reserved for game sanctuaries; 
(c) whether any plan is under consideration of Government to help 
State Governments acquire nearby land to sanctuaries; 
(d) if so, the details of such plans; and 
(e) the States which have been selected for this purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) There are no Game Sanctuaries, as such, in the country. 
Only four categories of Protected Areas, viz., National Parks, Sanctuaries, 
Conservation Reserves and Community  Reserves are there under the 
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. The National Wild Life Action Plan (2002- 
2016) envisages extension of Protected Areas from nearly 4.8 percent 
at present to ten percent of the country's geographical area. This will be 
achieved mainly through the establishment of Conservation Reserves 
in Government owned lands and of Community Reserves in community 
of private lands where the community or individuals volunteer to protect 
the wild life and its habitat. 
(c) to (e) Provision has been made under the Centrally Sponsored 
schemes of Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries, Project 
Tiger and Project Elephant for relocation, rehabilitation and acquisition 
of land for resettlement of people and to ensure habitat and corridor 
development of wild animals. Financial assistance for this purpose is 
provided to the State Governments on demand driven basis and subject 
to the availability of funds.

*163. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the progress of the work on broad gauge line 
between Lumding-Silchar sector of North-Frontier Railways; 
(b) by when this project is expected to be completed; 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
(c) whether Government will take initiative to provide the additional 
funds from DONER and other sources to complete the work; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) The gauge conversion of Lumding-Silchar-Jiribam and 
Badarpur-Baraigram is in progress. On Lumding-Silchar section, land 
acquisition for 342 hectare out of total 368 hectare has already been 
completed. Earthwork to the tune of 195.87 lakh cubic metres out of 
total 292.4 lakh-cum. and 181 bridges out of total 379 bridges have 
already been completed. Work on one tunnel is in progress and tenders 
for other 18 tunnels is under finalisation. The anticipated cost of the 
project is Rs. 1496.42 crore. An amount of Rs. 265.32 crore has been 
spent on this project upto 31.3.2004 and an outlay of Rs. 70 crore has 
been proposed in the budget 2004-05. 
(b) No target date of completion has yet been fixed. The completion 
of the project would depend upon availability of resources. 
(c) to (e) In the past, efforts were made to get additional funds 
from Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources. However, it had not been 
feasible to allocate additional funds for Railway projects from this pool 
due to other pressing demands of various States. Ministry of Development 
of North Eastern Region (DONER) have advised that funds through Non- 
Lapsable Central Pool are provided only to those projects which are 
submitted by the North Eastern States in their priority list. Normally these 
projects do not include Central Sectors like Railways.

Conversion of forest villages into revenue villages in Assam 
*175. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BR AHMA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of forest villages converted into revenue villages in 
Assam; 
(b) what is Government's policy to convert all forest villages, which 
have fulfilled the necessary criteria, into revenue villages; and 
(c) the steps, if any, to include some villages under forest village 
category which were settled before 1981 itself? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) No proposal has been received from the Government of 
Assam for conversion of forest villages into revenue villages. 
(b) The Central Government have issued policy guidelines on 
18-09-1990, under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, for conversion 
of forest villages into revenue villages. According to these guidelines, 
the Central Government may convert recognised forest villages into 
revenue villages on the basis of the proposal submitted by the concerned 
State/UT Government under the said Act. The Central Government would 
consider all land on which pattas have been issued prior to 25-10-1980 
by the authorised officers and the land is in continuous possession of 
the patta holders or their legal successors. These lands will include land 
under habitation, existing buildings, gochar lands, health centre, 
community centre, cremation ground, road etc. Further, it has also been 
clarified that the State Government  shall submit a map delineating the 
external boundaries of the areas wh ere pattas have been issued pre- 
1980. It should not be necessary for them to submit details of individual 
pattas. 
(c) There is no general provision to include villages not recognised 
as forest villages into the category of  forest villages. However, according 
to the said guidelines issued on 18-09-1990, certain specific habitations 
in forest areas which are more than twenty five years old, other than 
recognised forest villages, involving sizeable group of families, may be 
examined case by case on merits for their amicable settlement on the 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
basis of the proposal submitted by the concerned State/UT Government 
under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. Moreover, at present, legal 
status of forest land can not be changed due to the ban imposed by the 
Supreme Court of India on dereservation of forest land vide their order 
dated 13-11-2000 in W.P. No. 337 of 1995. 
Mobile diagnostic labs 
*176. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of mobile diagnostic labs which are functioning in 
different States of the country; 
(b) whether the lack of modern diagnostic technologies at the rural 
level leads to the death of millions of people, especially women; and 
(c) whether Government plan to have a big project with the help of 
NGOs to create a network of these mobile labs fitted with Ultrasound, 
Catscan and other facilities? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) The Central Government has no scheme 
under which mobile diagnostic laboratories are being run in rural areas. 
As per reports received from several major States, they too do not have 
any scheme for this purpose. Information about the number of mobile 
diagnostic labs functioning in different States of the country is, therefore, 
not available. 
(b) There is no available data linking the lack of modern diagnostic 
technologies at the rural level leading to the death of millions of people 
especially women. In Community Health Centres and even some Primary 
Health Centres and First Referral Unit s, laboratory with technicians are 
available to test blood, urine etc. relevant for ante natal care of expectant 
mothers. However, diagnostic t echnologies such as well-equipped 
pathology laboratories and ultrasou nd machines are available at the 
District hospital level, and' a CT scan is available at many of the tertiary 
hospitals, women requiring these inves tigations are referred to a higher 
level of health care where these facilities are available. 
(c) No. Sir.

Improvement in health services 
†*177. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any national norms in respect of the availability of health 
services have been prescribed for various States; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the availa bility of health services in a 
number of States is very deplorable as compared to other States; and 
(c) if so, the details of steps being taken to improve the state of 
health services in such States, pa rticularly in far-flung backward hilly 
areas? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) Population based norms have been 
prescribed for establishment of rural healthcare institutions, namely the 
Sub Centres, Primary Health Centres and Community Health Centres 
along with their staffing pattern and the norms are different for general 
areas and the tribal and hilly areas. Such population based norms have 
also been prescribed for ur ban healthcare infrastructure viz. Urban Family 
Welfare Centres and Urban Health Posts. 
(b) Differences in availability of hea lth services have been observed 
across states in terms of both establishment of public health institutions 
and staffing of the institutions vis-a-vis the norms as also due to shortage 
of essential drugs and consumables and lack of diagnostic and treatment 
facilities. 
(c) Health is a State subject and the responsibility of improving the 
state of health services primarily rests with the State Governments. 
However, the Central Government has been making every effort to 
increase its contribution to public health expenditure. The resources for 
public investment in health sector are being augmented by securing 
assistance from various bilateral and multilateral agencies for 
implementation of various disease control programmes. For improving 
primary healthcare services, the Tenth Plan goal is to establish primary 
healthcare institutions required to meet the healthcare needs of the 1991 
population as per the norms. For meeting needs of the growing 
population, the strategy is to strengthen the established institutions 
instead of opening new institutions.

45 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
Other steps taken by the Government include implementation of 
the national disease control programmes throughout the country for 
control of major diseases like Malaria, TB, Leprosy, AIDS, Blindness, 
Cancer and Mental Health. Also, norms for providing assistance under 
the various disease control programme s have been relaxed for remote, 
hilly and tribal areas. State Health Systems Project is being implemented 
with World Bank assistance in seven states to upgrade the secondary 
health infrastructure and provide qua lity healthcare services to the people, 
especially the rural poor and the under-served. 10% of the central sector 
health plan outlay is ear marked for the North-Ea stern States including 
Sikkim. In order to provide specialized medical care to the people of the 
entire North Eastern Region, the North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional 
Institute of Health and Medical Sc iences (NEIGRIHMS), Shillong is 
proposed to be upgraded to a 500-bedded super speciality referral 
hospital. Primary health is also one of the six components under the 
Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) wherein state are given 
Additional Central Assistance under the scheme for improving health 
services in the state. Also, it is proposed in the Union Budget 2004-05 
that new hospitals with 100 beds or more to be set up in rural areas 
would be entitled to a 100% deduction of their profits for a period of 5 
years.

*179. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Health Assembly had adopted a draft Anti- 
smoking Treaty with the support of 170 nations; 
(b) if so, whether India has subscribed and signed the treaty; 
(c) whether US, Germany and China ha ve objected to the treaty; 
and

and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
(d) whether the entry of the foodgrains and other essential 
commodities into the country from abroad will be controlled to safeguard 
the interest of the growers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The required information is 
given in Statement I and Statement II (See below): 
(c) With a view to encourage higher investment in agriculture and 
boost agricultural production, the Government announces in each season 
Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for major agricultural commodities. 
In order to protect the farmers from fall in market prices below the 
MSP level, the Government organizes purchase operations through 
public and cooperative agencies su ch as Food Corporation of India 
(Wheat, Paddy and Coarse Cer eals) and National Agricultural 
Cooperative Marketing Federation of India (NAFED), (Pulses and 
Oilseeds), besides other agencies designated by the State Governments 
for procurement of commodities for which MSP has been announced. 
The wholesale prices of agricultural commodities are constantly 
monitored and instances of market prices ruling below the MSPs are 
referred to the respective designated nodal agencies for undertaking 
procurement operations. 
Besides, the Farm Income Insurance Scheme (FIIS), which is under 
implementation on pilot basis, seeks to provide income protection to the 
farmers by integrating the mechanism of insuring production as well as 
market risks. 
(d) Subsequent to removal of quantitative restrictions on imports 
in 2001, the Government has increased import duties on a number of 
agricultural items to provide adequate protection to the domestic farmers. 
The import duties on wheat, rice, maize, edible oils, pulses, cotton, spices, 
tea, coffee, areca nut and apple have been increased in the last 5 years. 
The import of sensitive agricultural commodities is continuously 
monitored by the Government on regular basis. In the on-going 
negotiations on Agreement on Agriculture of World Trade Organisation 
(WTO), the Government is making all efforts to maintain necessary 
protection to the domestic producers from subsidized imports. Efforts 
are also being made to enlarge market access for export of Indian 
agricultural products.

(b) The research projects  initiated and on-going at Alapuzha Centre

531. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER

living below the poverty line. The per capita consumption norm has been 
fixed at Rs. 49.09 per month in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in 
urban areas at 1973-74 prices at national level corresponding to a basket 
of goods and service anchored on a norm of per capita calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas.

per month in rural areas and Rs. 454.11 per month in urban areas. 
(c) Under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), 35 kg

Distribution System is supplemental in nature and does not envisage

50% of the cereal requirement ev ery month for an average BPL 
household.

Reforms in sale management of agricultural products 
†535. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a great difference between the 
producer's cost and consumer price of the agricultural products in the 
country due to faulty management of sale of the same; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that a gap to the extent of 100 
per cent to 500 per cent in producer's cost and consumer price in a 
number of agricultural products has been found; 
(c) if so, Government's reaction in this regard; and 
(d) the measures Government are taking to make comprehensive 
reforms in the sale management of agricultural products? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): 
(a) and (b) The difference between the price received by producer and 
the consumer's price for agricultural commodities depend on various 
factors such as type of commodity, its perishability, distance from the 
consumer market, etc. Various studies conducted by the Directorate of 
Marketing and Inspection, Faridabad, an attached office of the Ministry 
of Agriculture has revealed that the producer share in consumer price 
in respect of foodgrains and oilseeds ranges from 65 to 70 per cent, 
while in case of vegetables such as potato and onion, it ranges from 
45 to 60 per cent. Recent study conducted by Confederation of Indian 
Industries has revealed that in the case of fruits and vegetables, farmer 
realizes less than 30 per cent of the final consumer price. 
(c) and (d) The agricultural marketing system in the country needs 
to be integrated and strengthened to enhance the share of farmers in 
the ultimate price of agricultural pr oduce. Towards this end, States 
have been advised to liberalize the law governing agricultural markets 
(APMC Act) to facilitate development of competitive markets by private 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
104 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
and co-operative sectors; allow pr ocurement of agricultural commodities 
directly from farmer's field and to establish effective linkage between 
the farm production and the retail chai n and Food Processing Industries. 
States have also been advised to provide institutional support to contract 
farming arrangements in which national and multi-national companies 
enter into contracts for marketing of agricultural produce as an effective 
method of linking small farmers to source of extension advice, seed, 
credit and to assured and profitable markets. At the National Conference 
of State Agriculture Minister held at New Delhi on 07.01.2004, all the 
State Governments agreed to review  their respective APMC Act for 
implementing the suggested reforms.

under the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP). The objective of

the rivers through the implementation of the following pollution abatement 
works:

flowing into the river through open drains and divert them for 
treatment. 
* Sewage treatment plants for treating the diverted sewage.

the use of wood and help in ensuring proper cremation of bodies 
brought to the burning ghats. 
River front development works such as improvement of bathing 
ghats etc. 
Other minor miscellaneous work like afforestation, public 
participation, public awareness etc.

in 157 towns along with the polluted stretches of 31 rivers spread over 
18 States at a total approved cost of Rs. 4688 crore including Central

Protection to marine environment 
545. PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ : Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that United Nations chose the World 
Environment Day, 2004 to focus attention on Marine Environment; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that India's Marine Environment has 
become vulnerable; and 
(c) if so, what measures Government have taken or envisages 
to take to protect marine environment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The marine environment throughout the world 
including India is facing challeng es. The Government of India has 
taken following steps for protection of the Marine Environment: 
* A National Committee has been constituted to advise the 
Government on policy guidelines for implementing 
programmes on conservation and management of wetlands, 
mangroves, and coral reefs. 30 mangrove areas and 4 coral 
reefs have been identified for intensive conservation and 
preparation of management action plans. 
* Coral reefs have been included in Schedule 1 of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
* All India Co-ordinated Project  on Coastal and Marine Bio- 
diversity launched during the year 1999-2000 envisages 
Survey and Inventorisation, Training and Capacity Building in 
Taxonomy and Establishment of Database Network. 
* A notification was issued in 1991 under the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986, regulating developmental activities in 
coastal areas falling in the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ). 
As per this notification, all the coastal States/Union Territories 
have prepared Coastal Zone Management Plans and are 
114 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
required to regulate development activities as per the 
provisions of this notification as amended from time to time. 
* Coastal Zone Management Authorities (CZMAs) have been 
constituted in all the coastal States/Union Territories to ensure 
implementation of the provisions of the CRZ Notification, 
1991. Similarly, National Coastal Zone Management Authority 
has been constituted to develop guidelines and review the 
progress of implementation of CRZ Notification, 1991. 
* A national contingency plan to deal with oil spill disasters has 
been prepared. India has ratified Marpol 73/78 and adopted 
the provisions in the Merchant Shipping Act. 
* The concept of Integrated Coastal and Marine Area 
Management (ICMAM) Programme has been launched to 
ensure the sustainable development of the coastal areas, 
rational utilization of marine resources, and proper 
management of the marine environment to prevent its 
degradation from developmental, commercial, or other 
activities. 
* The Coastal Shelterbelt Plantation Projects under Integrated 
Afforestation and Eco-development Project Scheme (IAEPS) 
envisage plantation in rows along the coastline to create a 
shelterbelt for checking soil erosion and sand ingress for 
protection of agricultural fields, roads etc. 
* Sunderbans in West Bengal, Gulf of Mannar in Tamil Nadu 
and Nicobar Islands have been designated as Biosphere 
Reserves. 
* The coastal stretches which are subjected to the pollution 
have been identified under Co astal Ocean Monitoring and 
Prediction System (COMAPS) study conducted by the 
Department of Ocean Development in the States of Gujarat, 
Maharashtra, Goa, Pondicherry, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Tamil Nadu, Orissa and West Bengal and Government of 
India has stipulated limits for discharge of wastes and also 
imposing zero discharge policies.

Health problems due to use of Endosulfan in Kerala 
554. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of villagers are suffering 
from serious health problems due to the use of Endosulfan in the 
plantation areas of Kasargod district in Kerala; 
(b) if so, the details alongwith the nature of diseases and the number 
of people affected so far; 
124 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether any compensation has been provided to the victims, if 
so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the details of steps taken by Government to protect the people 
in this area? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
According to a study report of July 2002, submitted by National Institute 
of Occupational Health, Ahmedabad which carried out an epidemiological 
study in Padre village of Kasargod di strict of Kerala, a possible link was 
found between the higher prevalence of various ailments including Neuro 
behavioral disorders, congenital malformation in female subjects and 
abnormalities related to male re-pr oductive system in the Padre Village 
with the aerial spray of Endosulfan.  However, Dubey Committee set up 
by Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperation, in its report of July, 2003, 
has concluded that there is no link established between use of Endosulfan 
in Plantation Corporation of Kerala (PCK) plantations and health problems 
reported in Padre Village of Kasar god Distt. of Kerala. The committee 
inter alia recommended to conduct compre hensive, well designed and 
detailed health and epidemiological study in entire cashew plantation 
area of Kerala to ascertain the incidence of diseases in Padre vis-a-vis 
Kerala State average and also in the event of incidence of unusual health 
problem to determine probable factors responsible for alleged health 
problems. It also recommended that use of Endosulfan be continued as 
per provisions of Insecticides Act 1968 but aerial spraying of Endosulfan 
may not be allowed in any situation including in PCK plantations to ensure 
full safety. Further, as per Governme nt of Kerala, an expert committee 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Dr. P.K. Sivaraman, Addl. Director 
of Health Services of Government of Kerala in its report submitted in 
August, 2003, has stated that it could not find any other reason other 
than Endosulfan spraying to explain the reported health hazard. The 
State Government temporarily banned aerial spraying of Endosulfan and 
declared pesticide holiday for five years. The Hon'ble High Court of Kerala 
in its order dated 12.8.2002 in O.P. No. 16300/01 has stayed the use of 
Endosulfan in the State. The State Government is providing free treatment 
to those, suffering from the reported problems and providing free 
medicine to the poor patients.

AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, 
Sir. The Drugs & Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2003 (Bill No. 93 of 
2003) further to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 was 
introduced on December 22, 2003 in the 13th Session of Lok Sabha. 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
(b) and (c) The salient amendments proposed under the Bill are 
given below:— 
1. It has been proposed in the Bill to enhance the punishments 
relating to spurious drugs upto a maximum of death penalty or 
imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 10 years 
but which may extend to imprisonment for life and shall also 
be liable to fine of one lakh rupees or upto three times the 
value of the goods seized, whichever is higher. 
2. Penalties for subsequent offenc es to be enhanced upto 10 
years and with fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees. 
3. Offences relating to spurious drugs to be made non-bailable 
and congnizable. 
4. Provision for setting up of special courts for speedy trial of 
offences relating to spurious or adulterated drugs. 
5. To confer powers upon police officers not below the rank of 
sub-inspector or other designated officer to institute 
prosecutions under the said Act. 
6. Provision for compounding of offences for minor offences under 
the Act. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the 
offenders involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The 
involvement of enforcing agencies like Police will help in speedy 
investigations to look the culprits and in controlling anti-social elements 
involved in such activities. 
(d) The said bill was introduced to control the menace of spurious 
drugs. Adequate provisions relating to the Good Manufacturing Practices 
and guidelines for clinical trials have been notified under the Drugs and 
Comestics Rules, 1945 made under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

activities undertaken by the Government for creating AIDS awareness

In the phase-ll of the National AIDS Control Programme, 
Government is giving the highest priority to an effective and sustained 
awareness campaign amongst the general population through 
Information, Education and Communication (IEC). The Government's 
programme for awareness general follows a multi media approach 
that includes television, radio, press print and outdoor publicity and 
interpersonal communication and advocacy. These are carried out 
extensively through linkages with media units of information and 
Broadcasting Ministry, and through intersectoral partnership with other 
ministries and sectors. The IEC activities have been undertaken 
through the 35 State AIDS Cont rol Societies, and 3 Municipal 
Corporation AIDS Control Societies, keeping in mind the need to 
respond to local priorities and communication in local languages.

programmes being conducted for the in school, out of school and 
rural youth as well as the college students, through the School AIDS 
Education Programme. The village Talk AIDS Programme, and the 
University Talk AIDS Programme.

National Institute of Occupational Health, Ahmedabad which carried 
out an epidemiological study in Padre village of Kasargod district of 
Kerala, a possible link was found between the higher prevalence of 
various ailments including Neuro behavioural disorders, congenital 
malformation in female subjects a nd abnormalities related to male re- 
productive system in the Padre village with the aerial spray of Endosulfan.

that residues of Alpha and Beta Endosulfan were found in soil and water 
samples too. However, Dubey Committee set-up by Ministry of Agriculture 
and Cooperation, in its report of July, 2003, has concluded that there is 
no link established between use of Endosulfan in Plantation Corporation 
of Kerala (PCK) plantations and hea lth problems reported in Padre village 
of Kasargod District of Kerala. The Co mmittee also found that in view of 
its no water solubility, high absorption to soil particles and ready and rapid 
microbial d-composition, it is not expect ed to travel long distance (from 
the treated areas) in the tropi cal environment. The committee inter-alia 
recommended to conduct comprehensive, well designed and detailed 
health and epidemiological study in entire cashew plantation area of 
Kerala to ascertain the incidence of diseases in Padre vis-a-vis Kerala 
State averages and also in the event of incidence of unusual health 
problem to determine probable factors responsible for alleged health 
problems. It also recommended that use of Endosulfan be continued as 
per provisions of Insecticides Act, 1968 but aerial spraying of Endosulfan 
may not be allowed in any situtation including in PCK plantations to 
ensure full safety. 
Further, as per Government of Kerala, an expert committee 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Dr. P.K. Sivaraman, Addl. 
Director of Health Services of G overnment of Kerala in its report 
submitted in August, 2003, stated that it could not find any other 
reason other than Endosulfan spraying to explain the reported health 
hazard. The State Government tem porarily banned aerial spraying of

coal and coke as well as high prices of these raw materials due to overall 
increase in demand for steel. 
(b) and (c) Government has no immediate plans to acquire coking

coal/coke in India and abroad and several proposals, thereof, are under 
consideration of SAIL.

Supply of raw materials to VSP 
608. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SI RIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Visa khapatnam Steel Plant of RINL is 
going to hit massively on profitability due to rise in input costs and non- 
availability of raw materials; 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that th e plant has been forced to tie-up 
for supply of coal and coke at triple the rates at which it was getting it 
earlier; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the action being taken or proposed to be taken to supply the 
necessary raw materials to VSP? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) The 
rise in input costs and non-availability of raw materials will affect the 
profitability of Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. (RINL), Visakhapatnam Steel 
Plant (VSP). However, the company is taking necessary action to source 
the required raw materials from the global market to maintain its steel 
production levels. 
(b) and (c) RINL (VSP) imports around 3 million tonnes of coking 
coal mainly from Australia, each year. In addition, it also purchases around 
4 lakh tonnes of Metallurgical Coke to supplement the in-house 
production of around 18 lakh tonnes of coke every year to meet its Hot 
Metal Production levels. From Februa ry, 2004 onwards, the coking coal 
and coke position in the global market became volatile both with respect 
to prices and availability. This was because of restricted issue of coke 
export licenses by China and some of the coking coal suppliers declaring 
force majeure in some Australian mine s. To safeguard the health of the 
steel plant and to maintain required production levels, RINL (VSP) took 
steps to source the minimum requirement of 2 2 lakh tonnes of coking 
coal and 1.8 lakh tonnes of coke from  global market at the then ruling 
spot prices which were three to four times higher than the prices 
contracted through long term agreements. 
(d) To meet the projected shortf all in coking coal and coke 
availability from long term agreemen ts the Company has contracted 
supplies by resorting to spot purchases. At the behest of the Ministry, a 
high level delegation consisting of senior officers of RINL and SAIL visited 
Australia in February, 2004 to explore alternative sources of supply of 
coking coal and to persuade long term suppliers to make additional 
supplies. The Company has also tied up, on long term supply contracts 
for coke for the year 2004-05. In the case of coking coal supplies have 
been tied up, on long term basis, with two out of three foreign supplies 
186

for 2004-05. In respect of other raw materials the Company is presently 
not faced with any problems with regard to availability.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Re: Criminal case against Shri Shibu Soren, M.P. 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): 
Sir, it has been reported in a section of the Press that Shri Shibu Soren, 
Union Minister of Coal and Mines had been involved in a murder case 
and that a warrant of arrest has been issued against him recently. 
It has been reported by the State Government of Jharkhand that 
Shri Shibu Soren is one of the accused persons in Narayanpur PS. 
Case No. 7/75 dated 24.1.1975 (G.R . 30/75) under sections 147/148/ 
149/302/436 IPC. It is further intimated by the State Government that 
the first information report in the above case was filed on 23.01.1975. 
As many as 69 persons were accused in the above case. All of 
them were chargesheeted together on  25.12.1979. Three persons were 
committed to Session Court for trial on 18.7.1986. Later, 56 persons 
were committed to Session Court for trial on 6.9.1986. These 59 persons 
did not include Shri Shibu Soren. A ll these 59 persons are facing trial in 
the court of learned Additional District and Session Judge (ADJ). 
Shri Shibu Soren is not facing trial in this case since he was not committed 
to Session Court for trial.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' RESOLUTION 
Extension of Reservation Policy Meant For SCs, STs AND OBCs 
to Private Sector 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI (Maharashtra): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I move the 
following Resolution: 
"Having regard to the fact that the founding fathers of our 
Constitution had made the provision of reservation for the Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes who were exploited and looked down upon 
in the Indian society since time immemorial to improve their lot and 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA) in the Chair] 
bring them at par in the society and to ensure that they too enjoy the 
benefits of nations fre edom and till recently these communities were 
having the benefits of re servation in Government services but due to 
disinvestments and privatisation of  public sector undertakings, banks 
and public utility services and ban on  creation of new posts and non- 
filling of vacant posts on a very large scale by the Union and the State 
Governments has made the reservation policy redundant, this House is 
234 

[16 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
of the opinion that the reservation policy meant for the SCs, STs and 
OBCs be extended to private sector also  in totality to protect the interests 
of these discriminated sections of our society." 
Sir, I have moved the Resolution, and my statements and 
observations on this Resolution would be in keeping with the Consti- 
tutional framework. 
Sir, you are well aware of the fact that there are many provisions in 
the Constitution that provide for reservation in favour of Scheduled 
Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes. I don't want to 
deal with them in depth. But I wish to quote some relevant Articles of the 
Constitution. 
Sir, Article 16-4(A) of the Constitu tion says, "nothing in this Article 
shall prevent the State from making any provision for reservation in 
matters of promotion to any class or classes of posts in services under 
the State in favour of Scheduled Ca stes and Scheduled Tribes, which in 
the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services 
under the State". 
While it is amply clear that the Constitution has incorporated certain 
provisions for reservation for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
in Government services, my Resoluti on relates to having the provisions 
of reservation being extended to the private sector also, for the SCs, 
STs and OBCs. With this objective, I have brought this Private Members' 
Resolution. 
Sir, dealing with the subject, there are certain misgivings in the 
society, and I want to clarify the position in this regard. The question is 
raised in certain sections of the society and the Press — for how long 
will the reservation policy continue? Sir, the misgiving is that, that 
reservation is a political reservation; that reservation has nothing to do 
with the reservation for the SCs, STs and OBCs. Many of us don't 
understand this misgiving. It is amply clear that what is provided for in 
the Parliament and legislatures is  a political reservation. For the 
reservation for SCs and STs incorporat ed in the Constitution, there is no 
time limit. For that, there is no time limit at all! So it should continue as 
long as discrimination persists when we talk of extending the reservations, 
we refers to political reservation. That is what we did when we extended 
it after every ten years from 1950-60, 1960-70, 1970-80, 1980-90 and 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004]  
1990-2000. This has nothing to do with the policy of reservation in 
employment as such, which aims at providing safeguard against 
discrimination as long as discrimination continues. Sir, this is one sort of 
misgiving. This misgiving has been dispelled in the Constitution itself. 
Article 340 evaluates the situation of the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes and OBCs as to how far they have achieved progress. 
Article 340 regarding appointment of a Commission to investigate the 
conditions of backward classes says, "The President may by order 
appoint a Commission consisting of such persons as he thinks fit to 
investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes 
within the territory of India and the difficulties under which they labour 
and to make recommendations as to the steps that should be taken by 
the Union or any State to remove such difficulties and to improve their 
conditions and as to the grants that should be made for the purpose by 
the Union or any State and the conditions subject to which such grants 
should be made, and the order appointing such Commission shall define 
the procedure to be followed by the Commission." The very purpose of 
this Article in the Constitution is to evaluate the progress that is being 
made after providing the reservation to the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes in the Constitution. This is some sort of evaluation. 
So, I have explained as to what were the misgivings in certain cross-sections 
of the society. I think this explains what sorts of misgivings they have. 
Sir, what is the theory behind providing reservation in the 
Constitution? What is the principle? The Chief Architect of the Constitution 
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar mentioned it. "It is nothing but a theory of the law of 
compensation." The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were kept 
from generations to generations aloof and excluded from basic human 
rights and right to development. They were excluded in many spheres 
and not allowed to join the mainstream of the society. Dr. Ambedkar 
observed, "it is the moral bounden duty of the society and the nation as 
a whole to see that the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are 
brought on par with the other progressive sections in society." This is 
the theory of compensation mentioned by Dr. Ambedkar. He said, "This 
is just to provide a bicycle to compensate the distance. When you go 
ahead, travel long, let him provide a provision like a bicycle to compensate 
and cover up the distance." This is the justification for reservation. He 
further observed, "It is not a matter of sympathy and pity. It is a matter of 
236

  DR. RADHAKANT NAYAK (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman. Sir, I thank

this Government has undertaken, and , therefore, the UPA Government, 
especially the Congress Party, as well as all the other Alliance parties, 
they all need to be congratulated on such a giant step.

but maybe, one or two points I propose to highlight. First of all, in today's 
world, affirmative action or reservation in posts, services and other 
resources is not a new idea. It has been reported in some of our judicial 
pronouncements by the Supreme Court. I remember a case in West 
Bengal, where a fishery ghat was auctioned, and the Supreme Court 
has come out in clear terms that t he principles of reservation should 
also extend in sharing of resources There are other pronouncements 
as well These are not limited to vacancies in posts and services only, 
but they extend to many other aspects of economic and social resources 
We have also some policy prescriptions with regard to resource 
redistribution. They were attempted during Mrs. Gandhi's time. I 
remember, if I am not mistaken it is the year 1970 or 1971 when the

indicating how at least 15 per cent of the water resources have to be 
reserved upstream for people who live above certain Rights of reservoirs

have been more or less forgotten. Ne vertheless, reservation in terms of 
resource allocations even in the case of natural resources also prevalent

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI BALWANT alias BAL APTE): We 
have a message from the Lok Sabha. 
Motion regarding constitution of the Joint Committee on offices 
of profit. 
SECRETARY-GENERAL: Sir, I beg to report: 
"that Lok Sabha, at its sitting held on Friday, the 16th July, 2004, 
adopted the annexed motion regarding Constitution of the Joint 
Committee on Offices of Profit. 
I am to request that the concurrence of Rajya Sabha in 
the said motion, and also t he names of the members of 
Rajya Sabha appointed to the Joint Committee, may be 
communicated to this House." 
MOTION 
"That a Joint Committee of the Houses to be called the Joint 
Committee on Offices of Profit be c onstituted consisting of fifteeen 
members, ten from this House and five from the Rajya Sabha, who shall 
be elected from amongst the mem bers of each House in accordance 
with the system of proportional representation by means of the single 
transferable vote: 
That the functions of the Joint Committee shall be— 
(i) to exmine the composition and character of all existing 
"committees" [other than those ex amined by the Joint Committee 
to which the Parliament (Preventi on of Disqualification) Bill, 1957 
was referred] and all "committees" that may hereafter be 
constituted, membership of which may disqualify a person for 
being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of 
Parliament under article 102 of the Constitution; 
(ii) to recommend in relation to the "committees" examined by it 
what offices should disqualify and what offices should not 
disqualify; 
273 

RAJYA SABHA [16 July, 2004] 
(iii) to scrutinise from time to time the Schedule to the Parliament 
(Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959, and to recommend 
any amendments in the said Schedule, whether by way of 
addition, omission or otherwise. 
That the Joint Committee shall, fr om time to time, report to both 
Houses of Parliament in respect of all or any of the aforesaid matters; 
That the members of the Joint Committee shall hold office for the 
duration of the present Lok Sabha; 
That in order to constitute a sitting of the Joint Committee, the 
quorum shall be one-third of the total number of members of the 
Committee; 
That in other respects, the rules of procedure of this House relating 
to Parliamentary Committees will apply with such variations and 
modifications as the Speaker may make; and 
That this House recommends to the Rajya Sabha that the Rajya 
Sabha do join in the said Joint Committee and to communicate to this 
House the names of the Members to be appointed by the Rajya Sabha 
to the Joint Committee." 
The above motion was adopted by Lok Sabha at its sitting held on 
Friday, the 16th July, 2004.
